## 12. Runtime periphery: lifecycle and orchestration
- V1 This chapter specifies the machinery that drives the loop itself, taking the loop of §10 and the data plane of §11 as given. [§10, §11]
- V2 §12.1 covers the control plane; §12.2 loop scheduling, in turn its wait primitive, its yields and the thread budget; §12.3 the next-snapshot wait; §12.4 the shutdown protocol; §12.5 scripts and the mid-run mutation doctrine; §12.6 the run lifecycle from `init!`, and partial advance; and §12.7 replay, where the trace re-drives the ordinary loop. [§12.1, §12.2, §12.3, §12.4, §12.5, §12.6, §12.7]

### 12.1 Control plane
- V3 The control plane (the separate few-word atomic surface carrying pause, pace and stop) is not staging, structurally (D-022). [D-022]
- V4 Staged writes apply at drains (the points where the loop applies staged device writes), and a paused loop drains nothing, so un-pause via staging would deadlock by construction.
- V5 Riding outside the drain/trace path is safe for determinism precisely because §10.7 put pacing (the pacer's wall-clock waits) outside the semantics (D-021). [§10.7, D-021]
- V6 Control changes when frames (iterations of the loop) execute, never what they compute, and stop merely truncates the trajectory.
- V7 This section covers, in order, when the loop reads the plane, the stop and its issuer, the pause, pace and `margin`, and the fields `Control` keeps.
- V8 Pause, un-pause, pace changes, `margin` changes and stop are a few scalar fields on that separate atomic surface.
- V9 The loop consults them at frame top, the start of each frame.
- V10 A change issued while a frame runs or waits is observed at the next frame top, at most one frame budget `h/p` later (D-269). [D-269]
- V11 The pause block, described with the pause verbs below, is the one wait that wakes at once.
- V12 The stop's issuers are the operator's channels and, in an interactive session, Ctrl-C.
- V13 The operator's channels are a front end's button, the handle of a device (any attached participant in the periphery) and calling code (D-310). [D-310]
- V14 An operator interrupt (Ctrl-C read as a control-plane stop) sets exactly this stop, with no separate entry point involved (D-132). [D-132]
- V15 The loop catches it at one of its unmask points, where a deferred Ctrl-C is raised (§12.4). [§12.4]
- V16 The stop word carries its issuer (D-203). [D-203] (bold)
- V17 The stop word is the control plane's stop request, one atomic word holding that issuer.
- V18 Each issuing site writes its identity (the device's name, `:code`, or `:interrupt`) by compare-and-swap from empty, and the first writer wins.
- V19 The loop's frame-top read consults the word for non-empty, so the recorded issuer is the request that actually initiated the tail, the ordered shutdown sequence of §12.4. [§12.4]
- V20 It lands in the termination record (the stopped-sim value naming how the run ended) as its `ControlRequestedStop` (§13.5, D-203). [§13.5, D-203]
- V21 `ControlRequestedStop` sits outside the stop policy (D-255). [D-255] (bold)
- V22 The policy is what the caller declares for one advance (§13.5). [§13.5]
- V23 The stop word is what anyone can issue at any moment.
- V24 The pause is two verbs on the simulation (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V25 `pause!(sim)` sets the pause flag and `resume!(sim)` clears it, from any task and in any lifecycle state.
- V26 `paused(sim)` reads it.
- V27 The loop consults the flag at frame top, so a `pause!` issued before `run!` starts the run paused at its first frame top.
- V28 While paused the loop blocks on a condition variable (notified on un-pause and stop), not a spin.
- V29 A stop issued while paused wakes the loop, which observes the stop word and enters the tail with no further frame (§12.4). [§12.4]
- V30 `step!` shares the frame top and blocks the same way, until `resume!` or a stop from another task.
- V31 A paused run is still running.
- V32 The lifecycle reads `running`, and the roster (the list of attached device entries) stays frozen (D-106). [D-106]
- V33 The tail clears the pause flag beside the sticky stopped status (D-268). [D-268] (bold)
- V34 The flag is never cleared at a run's start.
- V35 The stop word, by contrast, is cleared at the top of each run, because a stop belongs to the run it ended.
- V36 A pause left set by a run that stopped while paused would instead hold the next run at its first frame top, on a flag nobody remembers setting.
- V37 Clearing it in the tail removes that trap and keeps the start-paused spelling above.
- V38 The device handle carries no pause (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V39 Whether it gains the control verbs for the bridge is pending (`pending.md`, D-310). [D-310]
- V40 Pace and `margin` are two more verbs and two readers (D-269). [D-269] (bold)
- V41 `pace!(sim, p)` and `margin!(sim, m)` set them from any task in any lifecycle state, and `pace(sim)` and `margin(sim)` read them.
- V42 `margin` (§10.7) rides on the control plane for the same reason `pace` does. [§10.7]
- V43 It tunes the wait, never the arithmetic, so retuning the coarse/spin split mid-run is safe by construction.
- V44 `run!` and `replay!` take both as keywords and write them at entry.
- V45 Both are declared by the advance, as `t_end` is.
- V46 `pace` defaults to `Inf` and `margin` to 2 ms (Appendix B, D-133). [Appendix B, D-133]
- V47 `step!` takes neither and never waits.
- V48 A stepping session is the harness mode (§12.6), and its frames are bit-identical to `run!`'s by §10.7's invariant. [§12.6, §10.7]
- V49 `pace` is a positive real, `Inf` admitted, and `margin` a non-negative real, `Inf` admitted.
- V50 The two setters and the two keywords refuse anything else under `ArgumentInvalid` (Appendix C). [Appendix C]
- V51 Beside pause, pace and `margin`, `Control` keeps the stop word, the sticky stopped status, the running flag (D-317) and the wait (§12.3). [D-317, §12.3]
- V52 `Control` also keeps the shutdown tail's `join_timeout` (§12.4, D-256). [§12.4, D-256] (bold)
- V53 The lifecycle state is not stored, and `lifecycle(sim)` derives it (§12.6). [§12.6]
- V54 A run's outcome is not a control surface, so `termination` belongs to the `Run` (the state one run owns), not to `Control` (§12.6, D-255). [§12.6, D-255]
- V55 The control plane is what anyone may poke.

### 12.2 Loop scheduling: wait primitive, yields, thread budget
- V56 §10.7 fixed the shape of the pacer's wait, hybrid sleep-then-spin, and leaves the choice of the coarse phase's primitive to this section. [§10.7]
- V57 That choice is a scheduling decision rather than an arithmetic one.
- V58 It settles what else can run while a frame (one iteration of the loop) waits.
- V59 It is made here, together with the two questions that trail it, whether a frame is guaranteed to yield at all and how many threads a session needs.
- V60 The section ends with the liveness heartbeat that makes a starved device diagnosable.

#### The coarse phase's primitive
- V61 The coarse phase uses task-yielding `sleep`, and there is no `systemsleep` variant (D-027). [D-027] (bold)
- V62 What the choice buys is the wait slot.
- V63 `sleep` releases the loop's thread, which makes the pacer's wait the natural scheduling window for the co-resident tasks of devices (the attached participants in the periphery).
- V64 The design already spends that slot twice, as the staging slot (§10.7) and as what the drain (the frame-top swap that applies staged device writes) takes (§11.4). [§10.7, §11.4]
- V65 A `systemsleep` variant for dedicated-thread hard real-time deployments is a guarded addition (a capability the design admits but does not build).

#### The per-frame yield
- V66 With devices attached, every frame yields at least once (D-027). [D-027] (bold)
- V67 The rule is semantically free, because pacing (the waits inserted between completed frames), and hence yielding, is outside the semantics (§10.7, D-021). [§10.7, D-021]
- V68 The yield is implicit in the coarse-phase `sleep` whenever that phase runs.
- V69 An explicit `yield()` covers the frames where it does not run, namely unpaced runs and pure-spin frames with budget ≤ margin.
- V70 The spin phase itself never yields (D-027). [D-027]
- V71 Yielding there would trade its µs precision for scheduler noise.
- V72 The consequence is a bound on thread occupancy.
- V73 The loop holds a thread for at most one frame before the scheduler can run anyone else.
- V74 Julia's scheduler is cooperative, and the scheduler stall requires a thread monopolist, a never-yielding task that holds its thread forever.
- V75 That precondition is structurally absent from framework tasks.

#### The thread budget
- V76 The thread budget is a documented sizing rule and a startup warning, not a hard error (D-027). [D-027] (bold)
- V77 The scheduler stall FlightCore's `nthreads` error prevented cannot reproduce here, for two reasons.
- V78 The loop yields every frame.
- V79 Nothing couples a stall to anyone else, the GUI least of all.
- V80 It waits on nothing, ever.
- V81 It uses a snapshot acquire-load, its own staging cell and atomic control.
- V82 Under any starvation, then, the front end keeps rendering and the stop button keeps working.
- V83 Undersized sessions degrade to laggy inputs and stale snapshots, which are visible, recoverable states.
- V84 At `run!` or `replay!`, a run warns under `ThreadBudget` (Appendix C) when `Threads.nthreads()` is tight for the attached population, naming the `julia -t` remedy. [Appendix C]
- V85 That is one check per run, against the frozen roster (the list of attached device entries) (§11.3). [§11.3]
- V86 Tight means fewer threads than the roster plus one.
- V87 Every rostered device is a task, and the calling task (the task that invoked `run!`) hosts the loop, so a run occupies one task more than its roster (D-310). [D-310]
- V88 The sizing guidance behind the remedy is one thread for the loop and headroom for compute-heavy or blocking-ccall devices.
- V89 I/O backed by libuv (the I/O library under Julia's tasks) yields.
- V90 Raw blocking ccalls pin their thread for the duration.
- V91 There is no pinning and there are no sticky tasks.

#### The liveness heartbeat
- V92 Since starvation is survivable, it must be diagnosable (D-027). [D-027]
- V93 The record is the published framework status, the frozen diagnostics value each snapshot carries beside the table.
- V94 It includes per-device liveness (the liveness timestamp and the device's `task_state`) next to the pacer diagnostics.
- V95 The mechanism is the per-writer diagnostic cell, specified in full by §11.8, plus the device `Task` handles the loop already owns, and nothing besides (D-136). [§11.8, D-136]
- V96 The diagnostic cell carries the single liveness timestamp.
- V97 The loop reads `task_state` off those handles where it publishes (D-193). [D-193]
- V98 A starved, blocked or crashed device task shows in a front end as a stale heartbeat with a name on it, not as mysteriously frozen physics (D-310). [D-310]
- V99 `task_state` has three values (D-270). [D-270] (bold)
- V100 Outside a run every device reads `:none`.
- V101 Inside a run a device reads `:running` while its task lives and `:done` once that task has ended, whether the body returned or the wrapper caught its crash (§11.6). [§11.6]
- V102 A device whose `init!` threw, and so spawned no task, reads `:done` as well.
- V103 The record's crash count tells a crash from a return.
- V104 `orphaned` on a record is exactly `:done` (§11.7, D-270). [§11.7, D-270]
- V105 Stale means a liveness timestamp more than 2 s behind wall clock (D-133). [D-133] (bold)
- V106 The threshold is deliberately loose, because the heartbeat is advisory.
- V107 It is a liveness display and a record, never a kill trigger, never a detach.
- V108 It must also tolerate a device legitimately parked in a blocking read between rare data.

### 12.3 The next-snapshot wait
- V109 Rate-matched output devices (attached participants in the periphery), such as telemetry and disk streaming, act once per boundary.
- V110 A boundary is a published consistency point.
- V111 What they need from the framework is a way to learn that a boundary has happened without polling for it.
- V112 The next-snapshot wait (a device's blocking wait for the next publication) is that way.
- V113 This section gives its two artifacts, the loop's side, the device's side, its newest-wins semantics, and how the counter differs from the other two indices, in that order.
- V114 Two artifacts provide the wait, a monotonic boundary counter plus one `Threads.Condition` (D-028). [D-028] (bold)
- V115 The boundary counter is the loop's own.
- V116 It counts published boundaries, that is grid, `t` and boundary zero (the initialization boundary at `t₀`) (§10.1, §10.4), not frames. [§10.1, §10.4]
- V117 Consecutive wakes are therefore not necessarily `h` apart.
- V118 The loop's publication is `lock; counter += 1; notify; unlock`, nanoseconds of framework-only code.
- V119 Waiters never block it.
- V120 One parked in `wait` has released the lock as part of parking.
- V121 The order of the two publications is normative (D-114). [D-114] (bold)
- V122 The release-store of `latest` (the atomic reference readers acquire-load) (§11.2) happens before the counter increment under the lock. [§11.2]
- V123 [code block] # the loop, at every published boundary
- V124 The device side's predicate, `counter > last_seen` (below), therefore implies that `latest` holds at least that boundary, and a waiter can never wake onto a stale snapshot (the immutable per-boundary publication).
- V125 The converse is expected and correct.
- V126 A waiter may observe a newer snapshot than the increment that woke it.
- V127 Newest wins.
- V128 The device side is `wait_next_snapshot(handle)`, which blocks until `counter > last_seen && running` under the canonical predicate-loop idiom.
- V129 That idiom handles waiters at different paces, frames skipped while transmitting, and shutdown, all with no per-frame reset.
- V130 Shutdown works because §12.4 wakes all waiters and each predicate then routes its owner out (D-028). [§12.4, D-028]
- V131 The wait's semantics are newest-wins, no queues (D-028). [D-028] (bold)
- V132 A slow consumer skips boundaries and always receives the current world.
- V133 This mirrors the inbound side.
- V134 Inbound coalescing (the CAS merge that leaves one pending batch per device) keeps the newest level per face, and the wait delivers the newest snapshot, the same zero-order hold (ZOH) decision.
- V135 No backpressure exists in either direction, and the loop never waits on anyone.
- V136 Per-consumer every-boundary queues are rejected (D-028). [D-028]
- V137 A `Base.Event` latch is the wrong primitive here (D-028). [D-028]
- V138 Condition variables carry no facts, only "look again".
- V139 The facts that matter, the counter and `running`, live in state each waiter tests privately.
- V140 Two indices number the publications, and each lives in its own place.
- V141 The snapshot carries the trajectory's published-boundary ordinal with `t`.
- V142 Boundary zero is 0, and every publication after it, grid or `t`, counts one.
- V143 Any holder of a snapshot therefore indexes it without consulting the loop, whether the log or a post-run inspector.
- V144 A new trajectory restarts the ordinal at zero, with everything else `init!` resets.
- V145 The boundary counter is a different number.
- V146 It is the loop's monotone count of every publication it has ever made, never reset across trajectories, and its absolute value is nowhere normative.
- V147 It exists for the wait predicate alone, and it is never reset because a waiter's `last_seen` must never run ahead of it (D-230). [D-230]
- V148 An error's pointer for replay (the ordinary loop re-driven from the trace) is a third index, the frame-entry boundary index of §13.4, a frame count that names no `t` boundary (D-128). [§13.4, D-128]
- V149 The GUI does not use the wait.
- V150 Being VSync-paced, it reads `latest` at each render.
